sentences.text: The only material known of Gorgonavis alcyone is an isolated partial skull that includes the snout, lower jaw and a portion of the braincase.
The skull measures about 3 centimetres in length.
Fusion of the bones indicates that the individual had reached skeletal maturity at death.
In the premaxilla there are three or four pairs of teeth, a condition commonly seen in enantiornithean birds.
The rostrum is roughly two and a half times longer than the eye orbit, a proportion characteristic of longipterygid birds.
Three pairs of teeth are visible in the lower jaw, confined to the front of the snout.
At just 3 cm, the skull is tiny yet preserves fine details of the braincase.
Gorgonavis is the oldest known enantiornithean with a markedly elongated rostrum, dating to about 129.4 million years ago.
It represents the first longipterygid discovered outside of China, extending the group's known range to Europe.
Fossils of Gorgonavis were recovered from the Las Hoyas locality in Cuenca, Spain.
The holotype specimen, catalogued as MUPA-LH-13240, is curated at the Museo Paleontológico de Castilla-La Mancha.

The genus name alludes to the mythic Gorgons, especially Medusa, because only a skull fragment is preserved, while the species name references Alcyone, a figure transformed into a kingfisher with a long beak.
The elongated rostrum and tooth arrangement suggest a diet that may have involved probing for small prey.
Skull morphology places Gorgonavis within Longipterygidae, a family previously known only from Asian specimens.
Because the postcranial skeleton is absent, researchers treat its family assignment cautiously, noting that many diagnostic traits of Longipterygidae are found in the body skeleton.
Gorgonavis is assigned to the family Longipterygidae, which comprises two subfamilies, Longipteryginae and Longirostravinae.
The specimen exhibits a combination of characteristics from both subfamilies, making its precise placement within the family uncertain.
Gorgonavis lived during the Barremian stage of the Early Cretaceous, about 129.4 million years ago.
Paleontologists debate the exact relationships of Gorgonavis to other longipterygids because it shows a mosaic of traits from both longipterygine and longirostravine lineages.
